verses.zh: 无能的人蒙你何等的帮助！膀臂无力的人蒙你何等的拯救！
verses.en: “How you have helped[NOTE:1] the powerless![NOTE:2] How you have saved the person who has no strength![NOTE:3]
notes: These two chapters will be taken together under this title, although most commentators would assign Job 26:5-14 to Bildad and Job 27:7-23 to Zophar. Those sections will be noted as they emerge. For the sake of outlining, the following sections will be marked off: Job’s scorn for Bildad (26:2-4); a better picture of God’s greatness (26:5-14); Job’s protestation of innocence (27:2-6); and a picture of the condition of the wicked (27:7-23).

The interrogative clause is used here as an exclamation, and sarcastic at that. Job is saying “you have in no way helped the powerless.” The verb uses the singular form, for Job is replying to Bildad.
The “powerless” is expressed here by the negative before the word for “strength; power”—“him who has no power” (see GKC 482 §152.u, v).
verses.commentary:
26:2-3 Notice the parallelism.

- VERBS

- help (BDB 740, KB 810), Job 26:2a

- saved (BDB 446, KB 448), Job 26:2b

- given counsel (BDB 419, KB 421), Job 26:3a

- provided (lit. "caused to know," BDB 393, KB 390), Job 26:3b

- NOUN PHRASES

- "the weak" (lit. "him who has no power"), Job 26:2a

- "the arm without strength," Job 26:2b

- "to one without wisdom," Job 26:3a

This is all sarcasm! The subject "you" is SINGULAR, addressing Bildad
specifically.

verses.zh: 无智慧的人蒙你何等的指教！你向他多显大知识！
verses.en: How you have advised the one without wisdom,and abundantly[NOTE:1] revealed your insight!
notes: Heb “the arm [with] no strength.” Here too the negative expression is serving as a relative clause to modify “arm,” the symbol of strength and power, which by metonymy stands for the whole person. “Man of arm” denoted the strong in 22:8.

verses.zh: 你向谁发出言语来？谁的灵从你而出？
verses.en: To whom[NOTE:1] did you utter these words?And whose spirit has come forth from your mouth?[NOTE:2]
notes: The phrase לָרֹב (larov) means “to abundance” or “in a large quantity.” It is also used ironically like all these expressions. This makes very good sense, but some wish to see a closer parallel and so offer emendations. Reiske and Kissane suggested “to the tender” for this word. But the timid are not the same as the ignorant and unwise. So Graetz supplied “to the boorish” by reading לְבָעַר (lebaʿar). G. R. Driver did the same with less of a change: לַבּוֹר (labbor; HTR 29 [1936]: 172).

The verse begins with the preposition and the interrogative: אֶת־מִי (ʾet mi, “with who[se help]?”). Others take it as the accusative particle introducing the indirect object: “for whom did you utter…” (see GKC 371 §117.gg). Both are possible.
verses.commentary:
26:4 This verse has two questions. I think the NRSV catches the intended meaning.

"With whose help have you uttered words,

And whose spirit has come forth from you?"

Job is questioning the true source of Bildad's speech. The implication
is that it is from an evil, mistaken spiritual source. This may be the only
place outside Job 1-2 where "the adversary" is alluded to.

It is also possible that Job recognized that Bildad was alluding to
Eliphaz's previous speech (Job 4).

verses.zh: 在大水和水族以下的阴魂战兢。
verses.en: “The dead[NOTE:1] tremble[NOTE:2]—those beneath the waters and all that live in them.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “has gone out from you.”

This is the section, Job 26:5-14, that many conclude makes better sense coming from the friend. But if it is attributed to Job, then he is showing he can surpass them in his treatise of the greatness of God.

The text has הָרְפָאִים (harefaʾim, “the shades”), referring to the “dead,” or the elite among the dead (see Isa 14:9; 26:14; Ps 88:10 [11]). For further discussion, start with A. R. Johnson, The Vitality of the Individual, 88ff.
verses.commentary:
26:5-14 This is an extended
passage on the omnipotent God. I think it refers to the monotheistic
Deity of Israel. Monotheism is rare outside of Israel (i.e.,
Melchizedek, Gen. 14:17-24; and Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, Exod.
2:16-22; 3:1; 18:1-2, apparently knew of YHWH). Remember, I think a
Judean sage composed the book of Job based on oral traditions about a
historical person. Often, Israelite theology appears in the dialogues.

The attributes of God show

- His control over the dead, Job 26:5-6

- His control over creation, Job 26:7-13

- His hiddenness, Job 26:14

vol. 3, pp. 1173-1180.

▣ "under the waters"
Creation was thought to be established on the "cosmic waters"
(cf. Ps. 24:2; 104:2-3; 136:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

verses.zh: 在　神面前，阴间显露；灭亡也不得遮掩。
verses.en: The underworld[NOTE:1] is naked before God;[NOTE:2] the place of destruction lies uncovered.[NOTE:3]
notes: The verb is a Polal from חִיל (khil) which means “to tremble.” It shows that even these spirits cannot escape the terror.
Most commentators wish to lengthen the verse and make it more parallel, but nothing is gained by doing this.
Heb “Sheol.”
verses.commentary:
26:6 This verse asserts that God knows what occurs in Sheol
(BDB 982, i.e., holding place of the dead, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: Sheol) and Abaddon (BDB 2, cf. Job 28:22; 31:12;
Ps. 88:10-11; Prov. 15:11; 27:20; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABADDON. . .APOLLYON). Psalm 139:7-12, especially 139:8,
asserts YHWH is present in Sheol.

verses.zh: 神将北极铺在空中，将大地悬在虚空；
verses.en: He spreads out the northern skies[NOTE:1] over empty space;[NOTE:2] he suspends the earth on nothing.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “before him.”
The line has “and there is no covering for destruction.” “Destruction” here is another name for Sheol: אֲבַדּוֹן (ʾavaddon, “Abaddon”).

The Hebrew word is צָפוֹן (tsafon). Some see here a reference to Mount Zaphon of the Ugaritic texts, the mountain that Baal made his home. The Hebrew writers often equate and contrast Mount Zion with this proud mountain of the north. Of course, the word just means north, and so in addition to any connotations for pagan mythology, it may just represent the northern skies—the stars. Since the parallel line speaks of the earth, that is probably all that was intended in this particular context.
verses.commentary:
26:7 It is possible that "the north" (BDB 860) is a reference to
"the mount of assembly in the recesses of the north" (cf. Isa. 14:13; Ps. 48:2;
JPSOA footnote), which reflects Canaanite mythology of Mount Zaphon (other
mythology referred to in Job 26:12-13; see G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery
of the Bible, pp. 201-271).

However, Job 26:7 may be an alternate way of referring to the creation
of the earth.

- earth as a stretched tent (cf. Job 9:8; Ps. 104:2; Isa. 40:22; 42:5; 44:24; 45:12;
Jer. 10:12; 51:15) stretched over a void; hung on nothing (i.e., possibly
primordial ocean; i.e., Hebrew "Tohu," BDB 1062, cf. Gen. 1:2;

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH)

- earth built on subterranean pillars (1 Sam. 2:8; Job 9:6; Ps.75:3)

- John H. Walton, The NIV Application Commentary, Job,
p. 253, #35, suggests the word "earth" (BDB 75), which in this context,
means the netherworld (i.e., Sheol). He lists the other places where the Hebrew
word has this connotation (cf. Exod. 15:12; 1 Sam. 28:13; Job 10:21-22; Eccl. 3:21;
Isa. 26:19; Jonah 2:6).

verses.zh: 将水包在密云中，云却不破裂；
verses.en: He locks the waters in his clouds,and the clouds do not burst with the weight of them.
verses.commentary:
26:8-9 The two words for "cloud" (BDB 728 and BDB 777) are used in two senses.

- clouds that hold rain, so important for the agricultural societies of the ANE, Job 26:8

- clouds that cover God's glory lest mankind sees God and dies (i.e., Shekinah
cloud of glory), Job 26:9 (cf. Gen. 16:13; Exod. 33:20; Jdgs. 13:22; Hab. 3:4c; Isa. 6:5)

verses.zh: 遮蔽他的宝座，将云铺在其上；
verses.en: He conceals[NOTE:1] the face of the full moon,[NOTE:2] shrouding it with his clouds.
notes: There is an allusion to the creation account, for this word is תֹּהוּ (tohu), translated “without form” in Gen 1:2.
Buttenwieser suggests that Job had outgrown the idea of the earth on pillars, and was beginning to see it was suspended in space. But in v. 11 he will still refer to the pillars.
verses.commentary:
26:9

NASB
"He obscures the face of the full moon"

NKJV
"He covers the face of His throne"

NRSV, NJB, REB
"He covers the face of the full moon"

TEV
"He hides the full moon"

"He shuts off the view of His throne"

"He who holds firmly the face of the throne"

Peshitta
"He holds fast the covering of the firmament"

The UBS Text Project (p. 83) gives the NKJV an "A" rating. The
other option (NASB) has the same consonants but different vowels.

The basic meaning of the VERB
(BDB 28, KB 31) is to "seize," "lay hold of," or
"settle" (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 354-358). The Piel stem
is used of "hiding" or "covering." This covering
involves "the clouds" (cf. Job 26:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COMING ON THE CLOUDS.

▣ "spreads" This VERB
(BDB 831, KB 975, Pilel INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE)
occurs only here. It apparently comes from the VERB

verses.zh: 在水面的周围划出界限，直到光明黑暗的交界。
verses.en: He marks out the horizon[NOTE:1] on the surface of the watersas a boundary between light and darkness.
notes: The verb means “to hold; to seize,” here in the sense of shutting up, enshrouding, or concealing.
verses.commentary:
26:10 This verse refers to God's
separating the waters (i.e., salt and fresh in Gen. 1:9-10). God set a
boundary beyond which the waters may not pass (cf. Job 38:8-11; Ps.
104:9; Prov. 8:29). This shows God's power in creation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

verses.zh: 天的柱子因他的斥责震动惊奇。
verses.en: The pillars[NOTE:1] of the heavens trembleand are amazed at his rebuke.[NOTE:2]
notes: The MT has כִסֵּה (khisseh), which is a problematic vocalization. Most certainly כֵּסֶה (keseh), alternative for כֶּסֶא (keseʾ, “full moon”) is intended here. The MT is close to the form of “throne,” which would be כִּסֵּא (kisseʾ, cf. NLT “he shrouds his throne with his clouds”). But here God is covering the face of the moon by hiding it behind clouds.

The expression חֹק־חָג (khoq khag) means “he has drawn a limit as a circle.” According to some the form should have been חָק־חוּג (khaq khug, “He has traced a circle”). But others argues that the text is acceptable as is, and can be interpreted as “a limit he has circled.” The Hebrew verbal roots are חָקַק (khaqaq, “to engrave; to sketch out; to trace”) and חוּג (khug, “describe a circle”) respectively.
verses.commentary:
26:11-13 These verses describe
the power of God's spoken word (cf. Genesis 1). The "Rahab"
(BDB 923, meaning "pride" or "arrogance") of Job

26:11 "tremble" This VERB (BDB 952, KB 1279, Poal
IMPERFECT) occurs only here in the OT. Most English translations
translate it as "tremble." Some other options/guesses are

- swayed

- fluttered

- tottered

- quaked

but all convey the same basic thought.

verses.zh: 他以能力搅动（或译：平静）大海；他藉知识打伤拉哈伯，
verses.en: By his power he stills[NOTE:1] the sea;by his wisdom he cut Rahab the great sea monster[NOTE:2] to pieces.[NOTE:3]
notes: H. H. Rowley (Job [NCBC], 173) says these are the great mountains, perceived to hold up the sky.
The idea here is that when the earth quakes, or when there is thunder in the heavens, these all represent God’s rebuke, for they create terror.

The verb רָגַע (ragaʿ) has developed a Semitic polarity, i.e., having totally opposite meanings. It can mean “to disturb; to stir up” or “to calm; to still.” Gordis thinks both meanings have been invoked here. But it seems more likely that “calm” fits the context better.
verses.commentary:
26:12 is Babylonian creation mythology (for a good discussion of the
different ways the word "mythology" is used see G. B. Caird,
The Language and Imagery of the Bible, chapter 13, "The
Language of Myth") of God's destruction of watery chaos (cf. Ps.
74:12-17; notice it is parallel with Yam [sea], a god of ancient
mythology). This same theme may be carried over into Job 26:13. The
basic meaning of the word in 26:13a is "fair" (BDB 1051, KB
1636) but that does not fit the parallel of Job 26:13b, "pierced the
fleeing serpent." Perhaps the NASB, "cleared," TEV,
"clear," could reflect the context of Isa. 27:1.

▣ "understanding"
This Hebrew NOUN (BDB 108)
is personified in Prov. 2:9; 7:4; and 8:14. In Prov. 8:22-31 it is the
first creation of YHWH (i.e., Wisdom) whereby He created everything
else. This is a powerful word in Hebrew thought.

verses.zh: 藉他的灵使天有妆饰；他的手刺杀快蛇。
verses.en: By his breath[NOTE:1] the skies became fair;his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Rahab” (רָהַב), the mythical sea monster that represents the forces of chaos in ancient Near Eastern literature. In the translation the words “the great sea monster” have been supplied appositionally in order to clarify “Rahab.”

Here again there are possible mythological allusions or polemics. The god Yam, “Sea,” was important in Ugaritic as a god of chaos. And Rahab is another name for the monster of the deep (see Job 9:13).
verses.commentary:
26:13

NASB, TEV, NJB, NET
"His breath"

NKJV, Peshitta
"His Spirit"

NRSV, JPSOA
"his wind"

This is the Hebrew word ruah (BDB 924). As the Spirit was active in Gen. 1:2;
Ps. 104:30; Isa. 40:12-13, so too, in this cosmological text.

Because of Job 41:21, where Leviathan (another way to refer to Rahab) is
said to breathe out fire, some scholars (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 764) think
Job 26:13a refers to God defeating the ancient sea monster (i.e., watery
chaos, see
SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS). I think, in context, Job 26:11 and 13 all speak of the power of
the spoken word.

- His rebuke, Job 26:11

- He quieted the sea, Job 26:12

- His breath, Job 26:13

Notice the mention of "word" and "thunder" (imagery
of God's voice) is used in Job 26:14.

verses.zh: 看哪，这不过是　神工作的些微；我们所听于他的是何等细微的声音！他大能的雷声谁能明透呢？
verses.en: Indeed, these are but the outer fringes of his ways![NOTE:1] How faint is the whisper[NOTE:2] we hear of him!But who can understand the thunder of his power?”
notes: Or “wind”; or perhaps “Spirit.” The same Hebrew word, רוּחַ (ruakh), may be translated as “wind,” “breath,” or “spirit/Spirit” depending on the context.

Here too is a reference to pagan views indirectly. The fleeing serpent was a designation for Leviathan, whom the book will simply describe as an animal, but the pagans thought to be a monster of the deep. See the same Hebrew phrase in Isaiah 27:1. God’s power over nature is associated with defeat of pagan gods (see further W. F. Albright, Yahweh and the Gods of Canaan).
verses.commentary:
26:14 Of all the powerful acts of
God mentioned, they are only a mere fraction of His power and wonders.
He is beyond human comprehension (cf. Job 11:7-9; the book of Ecclesiastes).

▣

NASB
"faint a word"

NKJV, NRSV
"small a whisper"

NJB
"feeblest echo"

JPSOA

REB, NET
"faint the whisper"

LXX

This NOUN CONSTRUCT (BDB 1036 and 182) denotes a
fraction or fragment of something (cf. Job 4:12). This word (BDB 1036)
occurs only twice in the OT, both in Job. The parallelism with "fringes"
(or "outskirts of," BDB 892) drives the translation options.

▣ "His mighty thunder"
God uses sound to communicate His presence and power. This verse relates
to Job 26:11, "His rebuke."

Notice the ways God shows His presence (using different synonymous
roots).

- thunder – Exod. 9:23,28,29,33,34; 19:16; 20:18; 1 Sam. 7:10; 12:17,18;
Job 26:14; 28:26; 38:25; Ps. 29:3; 77:18; 81:7; 104:7; Isa. 29:6

- lightning – Exod. 19:16; 20:18; 2 Sam. 22:15; Job 28:26; 37:3;
38:25; Ps. 18:14; 77:18; 97:4

- flames of fire – Exod. 3:2; Jdgs. 13:20; Ps. 18:8; 50:3; Isa. 29:6; 30:30;
66:15; Joel 2:5

- wind – Gen. 8:1; Exod. 10:13,19; 14:21; Num. 11:31; 2 Sam. 22:11;
1 Kgs. 19:11; Job 1:19; 38:1; Ps. 18:15; 48:7; 104:3; 135:7; 147:18; Isa. 29:6;
66:15; Jonah 1:4; 4:8

Just a closing thought on this cosmological poem, God, the one true God,
is powerful! However, in all this power (i.e., creation), Job is still
sick and rejected. He affirms God's power and sovereignty but questions
His fairness and justice. God reveals Himself to Job in power at the end
of the book (Job 38:1-40:6), but never answers the questions about His
justice! It remains the mystery of evil in a world created by,
controlled by, guided by an all-powerful and loving God. The mystery
remains!! See Contextual Insights A and B at Job 38.

- Explain the word "mythology."

- Why is Job 26:9 so difficult to translate?

- Who is Job 26:13 talking about?

- Explain in your own words the implication of Job 26:14.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- See note at Contextual Insights of Job 25.

- Job's response to Bildad is very sarcastic. Job feels that his three comforters
have not only not brought comfort but have attacked him unfairly.

The Jewish Study Bible (p. 1537) thinks Job 26:2-4 is from Bildad
because of the use of the SINGULAR "you."
Everywhere else Job uses the PLURAL "you," but
the three comforters always use the SINGULAR.

- Job 26:5-14 "may" be part of Bildad's speech. This section of the
dialogues does not match the other cycles. Why is uncertain.

They seem to continue the thought of God's greatness begun
in Job 25:1-6. However, 26:5-14 is a wonderful poem of God's greatness and
could surely be from Job. This type of cosmic imagery does not fit Bildad's
previously recorded words.

- This cosmology reflects the thought of ANE cultures (see Introduction to
Genesis online). It was a three storied worldview.

- The atmosphere was a dome with several levels (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN).

- The dry ground was a flat disk floating on water (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: CIRCLE OF THE EARTH).

- The dead were beneath the dry ground in a prison house (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL).

For a good discussion of Semitic cosmology see John H. Walton, Lost World of
Genesis One and ANE Thought and the OT: Introducing the Conceptual
World of the Hebrew Bible.

- There are several places where ANE creation mythology (i.e., conflict with watery chaos) is alluded to.

- Job 9:13 – Rahab

- Job 20:12-13 – Rahab; the fleeing serpent

- Ps. 74:12-17 – sea monsters; Leviathan

- Ps. 89:9-10 – Rahab

- Ps. 104:25-26 – Leviathan

- Isa. 51:9-10 – Rahab; dragon

See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, chapter
13, "The Language of Myth."
